subject: Agriculture
title: Terrace Farming
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Terrace Farming.

hook.text: Mountains are terrible for farming. Unless you carve them into staircase-like terraces.

buildup.text: The Inca built terraces across the Andes, turning steep slopes into flat, irrigable planting surfaces.

discovery.text: Terraces trap rainwater, prevent erosion, and create microclimates—warmer at the bottom, cooler at the top.

twist.text: The Ifugao Rice Terraces of the Philippines are 2,000 years old and still in use today.

climax.text: Maintaining terraces requires constant labor. When people leave, terraces crumble and hillsides erode.

punchline.text: Terrace farming turns mountains into farmable stairways.

quiz.question: What is the primary benefit of terrace farming on steep slopes?
options: Flat surfaces trap water and prevent erosion

details.summary: Terrace farming carves steep hillsides into stepped, flat platforms for crop cultivation. This topic covers terracing techniques from the Andes to Southeast Asia, how terraces conserve water and prevent erosion, and their continued importance in mountain agriculture.
details.whyItMatters: Terracing transforms otherwise unusable steep land into productive farmland. For millions of mountain communities worldwide, terraces are the only way to grow food on the landscape they inhabit.
takeaways: The Inca terraces at Moray in Peru may have served as agricultural laboratories
Rice terraces in the Philippines are over 2,000 years old and still in active use
Terracing reduces soil erosion by up to 90% compared to farming on slopes

faq.question: How does terrace farming work?
faq.answer: Farmers cut horizontal steps into hillsides, creating flat platforms retained by stone or earthen walls. Each terrace captures rainfall, slows water runoff, prevents soil erosion, and creates level ground suitable for cultivation on otherwise steep terrain.

faq.question: Where are the most famous agricultural terraces in the world?
faq.answer: Iconic terraces include the Banaue Rice Terraces in the Philippines, Inca terraces at Machu Picchu and Moray in Peru, Longji terraces in China, and terraced vineyards along the Douro River in Portugal and the Rhine in Germany.
